newsitem.title: USA: Economist disputes Miami, Fla., deficit figure.
newsitem.headline: Economist disputes Miami, Fla., deficit figure.

text.p: An economist for Miami, Fla.'s labor unions said Monday he estimated the city's fiscal year 1996 deficit was only $8.7 million, less than half of the $19.4 million projected by the city.
Economist Larry Jessup said city revenue exceeded estimates by $6 million while expenses were $3.4 million less than projected for the fiscal year that ended Sept 30, 1996.

Speaking at a committee meeting of the Miami oversight board, Jessup said his estimate was based on a two-month review of data provided by the city. Jessup cautioned that his figures were not final because the city still has not finished posting all its payments for fiscal 1996.
But Treasurer Pete Chircut said the amount still to be posted was probably less than $1 million.
After the meeting, Jessup said city officials were "working off the Chicken Little-the-sky-is-falling mindset" in order to squeeze more cnocessions from union workers.

The city's four employee unions have agreed to $25 million of concessions, which expire at the end of 1998. But in order to produce the five-year budget required by the state-appointed oversight board, the city must begin preliminary wage negotiations now.
Jessup agreed to sit down with city manager Ed Marquez and city financial advisers to explain his lower estimate of the budget gap.
Marquez said, "I hope they are absolutely right and our overall problems may be less."
"I think we should explore it," said oversight board member Cynthia Curry.

The city expects the official and final figure for the 1996 deficit when its outside auditor, KPMG Peat Marwick, finishes its report by the end of March. The auditor has said the final deficit number could change from current projections.

Jessup also suggested during the meeting that Miami has about $7 million in excess revenues in its debt service accounts, and may be able to use some of that money to offset the deficit, if the bond documents permit other uses of the revenue.
Marquez was skeptical of that figure, and said the money Jessup referred to may be reserves that the bond documents require the city to hold.
